title: The Surrender
text:
Because the body,

the whole body, sheltering life within it

its dark though illustrious omnipotence,

is always here, will always be.

And whoever loves and whoever desires wants

to possess and surrender while possessing.


Afternoon and night, dawn or morning,

for love, loving lays claim to the body

in a gentle passage, or turbulent

along a path brimming with lava:

the shadowy eternity that gives life

a death embedded within it.


A frozen volcano; are they oceans,

lucid and vertiginous,

with the fury of dying while I love?

For such is the surrender of the lover:

a despotic catastrophe.


Am I like this, am I this, one asks oneself,

growing from a savage crossroads,

living on my death, which I reclaim,

with the fury of dying when I love?

The body listens meekly within,

and another self suffocates in the question.


How untouched the awakening. Now divesting itself,

the invasion of itself, the body moans.

The sea returns, absorbent, claiming it,

and once again it collapses and recovers.
editorial_note: Translated from the stored Spanish original. The body’s shifting relation to life, death, possession, and surrender, along with the poem’s reflexive ambiguities, is preserved.

title: Song to the Firstborn Son
text:
Son of the earth,

the Garden cast you out.

Though you see shadows,

do not seek to shine.


Your mother was beautiful;

the winds dry her out.

Your mother was tender;

she burns in the wasteland.


Your mother was biting

the apple tree’s flower

when man placed

your life in her hand.


Your mother sowed

the rye with you

while you drank

the milk from her bowl.


Son of the wrath

of implacable God.

Your mother cannot save you

from hatred.


Do not sleep, keep watch.

Do not sleep, awaken.

Cold, the barren inheritance

threatens you.


Eyes pursue you

without sweet respite.

The Creator’s eternal hand

hates you.


The gazelles run:

you will run faster.

The lions leap:

you must leap.


The streams flee:

you have to flee.

Though I wish it otherwise,

you cannot sleep!


Do not sleep, listen.

Do not sleep, lie in wait.

The birds will whistle

over drunken branches


to make this dark earth

light for you.

Listen to me, son:

do not sleep, do not sleep…


For all the ages,

do not sleep,

do not sleep!
editorial_note: Translated from the stored Spanish original. The Edenic imagery, maternal address, imperative refrain, and stark alternation of tenderness and threat are preserved.

title: The Universe Has Eyes
text:
They look at us;

they see us, they are seeing us, they look at us,

multiple invisible eyes we have long known,

from every corner of the world. We feel them

fixed, shifting, enslaved and enslaving.

And sometimes they suffocate us.


We would like to scream, we scream when the nails

of the endless vigils harry and exhaust us.

They fulfill their mission of looking at us and seeing us;

but we would like to slip our fingers between their eyelids.


So that they might see,

so that we might see face to face,

eyelashes against eyelashes, evading the breath

thick with unease, fear, and longing,

the absolute vision we all pursue.


Ah, if we could surprise them, made tangible,

meeting on the fluid surface of the mirror!


They will look at us forever,

we know it.

And we will walk gathered together, without finding ourselves as mortals,

around the same intact creature

that rejects the eyes it has created.

Why, if we are not going to see it, though it blind us,

did it make those and these innumerable eyes?
editorial_note: Translated from the stored Spanish original. Two evident transcription errors are silently regularized: ‘vemos’ as ‘vernos’ (‘seeing us’) and ‘en tomo’ as ‘en torno’ (‘around’).

title: Gazes Are Trees Shedding Their Leaves…
text:
Gazes are trees shedding their leaves.

We must enter what is compact,

bore through the mystery to discover the ground

covered with poplars, with elms,

with web-footed cedars.


The dense vegetation bows beneath the weight of time

its radiant abundance, moist with ethers…

Ah, the hurtling impetus

of the branches, of the gazes

cutting themselves from their trunks!


Hardly anything, hardly the acrid vapor released

by the teeth of the implacable flock

when it bites the pasture…

Invisible smoke of torn greenery,

a warm plume of scents.


We lose them, unconsciously cutting them away

through long contemplation.

And we are left in deserted lands,

on ravaged shores,

in counterfeit oases without water or palms.

Why, until when, at what moment

will all those gazes gather in a quivering sheaf,

to become one brief, definitive ray?


This viscous, slippery ground,

the tides of leaves that were eyes

clinging to things, to beings, to the illusion of seeing!
editorial_note: Translated from the stored Spanish original. The sustained fusion of gaze and vegetation is kept literal, including the strange ‘web-footed cedars’ and the sheaf/ray transformation.

title: Those Men of the Violin Carry Their Voice in Their Arm…
text:
Those men of the violin carry their voice in their arm

like the firm vein of a young girl’s song.

Sweetly they guard it, their eyes closed,

all ember and sigh from the dream that rains

a tiny dew of captive flowers

onto the fragrant bodies of their musical violins,

still bearing leaves and aromas from the blazing forest.


A violin is the voice of a fountain with wind,

ruffled by gusts both harsh and most sweet.

The one who plays it knows, and his hair floats

like grass climbing the trunk of a tree,

while one hand pushes the strings toward the sky

and the other travels a zodiac with the bow.


It is golden; it smells of tuberose in the moonlit night,

and sows the forsaken afternoon with jasmine.

As slender and light as the nymphs once were,

sinuous and seaweed-clad, like a green mermaid.

It is the voice the cold Spring prefers.

And it tells Autumn that the birds have gone.

The cypresses exhale it. The warmth of flights

in the violins joins the nests with the feathers.
editorial_note: Translated from the stored Spanish original. The apparent transcription ‘En rubio’ is read as the contextually clear ‘Es rubio’ (‘It is golden’); the instrument’s animate and woodland imagery is otherwise preserved.

title: Lover
text:
It is like laughing inside a bell:

without air, without hearing you, without knowing your scent.

With a gesture you wear away the night of your body

and I make you transparent: I am you for life.


Your eyes do not end; the others are the blind ones.

They do not join you to me; no one knows that yours

is this mortal absence falling asleep in my mouth

when the voice cries out in deserts of weeping.


Tender laurels sprout on other brows,

and love consoles itself by lavishing its soul.

All is light and faintness where children are born,

and the earth is made of flower and in the flower is a heaven.


Only you and I (a woman at the back

of that lusterless glass that is a hot bell)

keep considering that life…, life

can be love, when love intoxicates;

it is surely suffering, when one is happy;

it is surely light, because we have eyes.


But to laugh, to sing, to shudder, free

to desire and be so much more than life…?

No. I know now. Everything is something I once knew,

and because of it, because of you, I remain in the World.
editorial_note: Translated from the stored Spanish original. The bell and glass images, the shifts between second and third person, and the poem’s paradoxes of happiness, suffering, and light are preserved.

title: Sahara Desert
text:
Yes. I once had a sea above my sand.

A great sea without limits, compact.

The golden land that scorches solitudes

was august and swollen with the sea I am no longer.


Gulls pecked at my swaying body,

ships moved over my waves.

For I was the sea that boiled above the golden sand,

the saturated sand that now cries out for its water.


Oh, the sea here as phantom, the sea the wind feigns

by unbraiding dunes as it winnows my sand!

Oh, sea of dense water, bodily and hard,

for which travelers through my soft desert yearn!


What archangels of fire could have evaporated

so much sea as I had, carrying it into an abyss?

My scorched sand is the thirstiest mouth,

crying out for water the gods drank from it.


Men walk across me, dreaming I am peopled

by that sea which was mine, the sea above the desert.

I soften my flesh for them, my sand receives them,

and they complain of thirst beside my breathless thirst.


Oh, sea of my genesis, the sea they drained from me

into a trench of flames: how heavy the sand is!
editorial_note: Translated from the stored Spanish original. The desert speaks throughout as the former sea. The apparent transcription ‘sede’ is read as ‘sed’ (‘thirst’), supported by the stanza’s repeated thirst imagery.

title: Enclose You in Words…
text:
Enclose you in words…

That you, you, should fit into verbs, nouns,

and untouched adjectives!

That I might say everything:

what is ours, this that we do

and will go on doing always,

for all eternity:

speaking, keeping silent, being you and I

by making ourselves each other’s.


Give you a human dimension,

a likeness of you on earth:

statue, color, impassioned step,

and serene gaze with those eyes of yours

and mine: our gaze upon the world.


That one day, mortals beyond all remedy may know

how you had blood,

and an open passion for everything;

and gave yourself singing, suffering,

to my mad, and slow, and weak arms,

and strong, and cold, and poor in light,

but in love with you.

So they may know that you were true,

that you were, but then you are no more!


To seek the words for when you do not live,

so that you may live while speech remains.

God of sorrow, I will never be able to say

what you are like, my love, love of mine,

creature of glorification whom I find

poured across oceans,

skies, fields, rivers, and trees;

and even in sad doves that at dawn

wake you to my love for you!
editorial_note: Translated from the stored Spanish original. The recursive language of naming, mutual belonging, future absence, and survival through speech is preserved.

title: Now You Will Begin, My Life…
text:
Now you will begin, my life,

to keep me from living.

To make the days and their nights nothing but

the fierce suffocation of encountering you.

Of your incorporation into me,

of your clothing yourself in me.

To keep my blood from knowing how to stop on its own,

and make it hurl itself toward yours, toward you,

with the furious joy of loving you,

with the ecstasy of knowing itself yours;

and with the anguish,

with the tremendous dark miracle

that is belonging to you!


Now yes; now.

When no one seeks me, nor do I seek.

Because your voice fills the earth with lofty echoes,

and your scent the most shadowy gardens,

and from your chest fall the bells of my desires

for you, for myself whom through you I regain,

and I learn, my life, my soul, my love,

that it is true I am made of flesh,

that it is true I ache,

and rejoice, and suffer, and cry out

because I am yours.


Exhausted moment of the world,

this in which I know you are far from me!


Drain it all, return to our abyss

and leave me submerged in you,

a force given to you without tears

of rebellion; though with violent weeping

at seeing myself yours,

I who belonged to no one,

not even ever to myself!,

your slave, given to you, lover.
editorial_note: Translated from the stored Spanish original. The speaker is feminine; the poem’s syntax of blood, embodiment, belonging, and self-recovery through the beloved is preserved.

title: First Love
text:
What a surprise your body is, what ineffable vehemence!

For all this to be yours, to be able to enjoy everything

without having dreamed it, without even

a faint hope ever promising happiness.

This fiery happiness that empties your head,

that thrusts you backward,

knocks you into an abyss

without measure or bottom.

Abyss and abyss alone

from yourself until death!

Your arms!

Your arms are the same as on other days,

and they tremble and close around your body.

Your breast, the one that sighs, estranged, trembling

with things you do not know,

with worlds that move it…

Oh, breast of your body, so firm and so sensitive

that a breath clouds it

and a kiss pierces it!

If no one ever said one could love so much like this!

Could you have expected your hair to burn,

all that you are to fall like flame

in an unnumbered cry,

from a mountain range cried out by the dawn?


Ash one day, you? Ash, this madness

you inaugurate with life newly sprung into the world?

You never end, you never go out!

Here is the blaze, the one that seizes everything

to burn the sky by raising the earth to it.
editorial_note: Translated from the stored Spanish original. The speaker’s self-address and abrupt shift to ‘his body’ are retained, as are the abyss, fire, and mountain imagery.

title: When the Day Still Has Enough Left to Go On Being Beautiful…
text:
When the day still has enough left to remain most beautiful,

a rose-colored blood that delicately tints the world,

brings the hills to life, flushes the coves where the sea reclines,

and lays its hands amid the unexpected gray of clouds,

the farmers return from work…


In their short, sweat-soaked shirts,

in their patched trousers dirty with earth,

but with bodies bathed in the scent of the sea,

and eyes blue with a sky lit pink,

and a weariness indifferent to anything but going

in search of sleep…


Oh, the slow afternoons of the Mar Menor!

The indelible terraces of water wetting themselves with moonlight

and the surf-less dusks beating arrhythmically.

The women walking slowly, astonished by maternities

that never cease; and children of fleeting, agile forms

with a piece of the future between their teeth.


Pink poured out in a torrent of frenzied beauty.

Pink of the working day and of the leisure that contemplates,

and of the small, rugged beaches by which

eternal eyes escape in a purification of life.


Oh, sea of my land, oh, sea of Palestine!
editorial_note: Translated from the stored Spanish original. The collection-and-date footer is omitted as bibliographic matter; the poem’s long opening sentence, repeated pink light, and final identification of seas are preserved.

title: Builders at the Mar Menor
text:
Because everything is the same, because it will always be the same,

they pass and smile, they pass and move away with their identical days

on backs tired from bowing beneath sun and labor…

They build houses for others, for those who come from far away

seeking rest or leisure, contemplation or sleep,

ecstasy of sea and of blue, pink, and violet sky.


Old and serene, young and ardent, new and panting,

all those who carry stones back and forth

are the same who, millennia ago, raised

pyramids and temples for sacrifices to the gods

at the command of others; with the same sweat and thirst.


Without the alien, indifferent command to build,

everything, everything would be as on creation’s first day.

Ground and sky, sea and pines, fruits and birds, fallow land

and land freshly turned today,

in an immense, empty calm, a calm ignorant of itself.


This great peace of immortal glory is secured

(oh, sublime sorrow of so many human certainties!)

at the cost of the effort and renunciation of those who take from the furrow

a piece of bread before the round sea

which is now radiant, my aboriginal sea.

I am nothingness.
editorial_note: Translated from the stored Spanish original. The collection-and-date footer is omitted as bibliographic matter; the historical parallel between modern builders and ancient laborers is preserved.

title: Flight in the Gardens
text:
The youngest, desiring you, advance

down these avenues of fragrant trees.

They escape a spring that tarnishes the flowers

with an ardor smelling of fruit, of stallions…

What a wild presence these pubescent females have

among warm wisteria, among vivid mock orange!

They demand to be loved, to be chased at a run

so joys may be poured over them on the drunken shore.


Girls, run faster: run until dawn!

These great males with their heaving chests

long to shell you, oh, crackling ears of corn!,

with their hunger of mouths and their hunger for fruit.

Even the river, a cut that marks the bounds of dreams,

smells of love and feasts…


The poplars trembled when there burst as one

the dark heartbeats of paired nightingales.

The laps of moss, the chill of the rushes,

watching the encounter, quicken their green.

It is a trembling canticle, swallowed in throats

by love opened in the heart of the forest.


Run always, girls, for following you excites

the ardor in men of catching you, all theirs,

men who brandish only the gesture of fierceness!

And wrap yourselves in garments of pure white linen

to wet those hot bodies with them,

and at dawn be girdled, before the love that throbs,

by the zeal of water, possessor of virgins.
editorial_note: Translated from the stored Spanish original. The evident transcription ‘a amor ya festines’ is read as ‘a amor y a festines’ (‘of love and feasts’); the poem’s pursuit, fertility, and water imagery is otherwise preserved.

title: There Are Fluid Pains, the Color of Blood
text:
There are fluid pains, the color of blood,

that pass gently, lightly from the chest.

And there are dark pains, sinuous, so slow

that little by little they soak us until we are drunkenly full.


Pains of madness, like accursed wines

that hurl us, blind, into the murky abundance

of an anguish without law, without an end, without an echo!


And that viscous pain, like a black liquid,

thick and slippery, dense blood, already dead,

that advances over the floor of our being…,

that advances and leaves cold the marble floor

that we who grieve are, seeping through it;

pains that riddle this vulnerable skin

of the defenseless soul, when He does not shield it;

pains that little by little make us numb,

pains without a fold, pains of armor.


And that compact pain, a clot of bitumens

that fire melted and now moves slowly,

leaving us dyed with a night without dawn?


That pain of the prisoner awaiting death,

seized by shackles, by chains that will not break!

That pain of the neck awaiting the stroke

of an axe that cuts though a mother prays.


That pain so broad, so steadily growing, is mine:

the one my nape endures as it remains pinned

by the mass of black blood, dead, unceasing…


Stop the blind world, stop it in the morning

of a morning open like a whole rose!

Stop, for pity’s sake, for my pain spills over

and all I am is a puddle of screams of agony!
editorial_note: Translated from the stored Spanish original. The progressive thickening of pain from fluid blood to armor and bitumen, and the final bodily dissolution, are preserved.

title: There Is Barely Distance, Barely between the Fields…
text:
There is barely distance, barely between the fields

the sea and sky add up to form far reaches…

Everything is close, hands can reach everywhere.

Only being beside you is deep; you are not.


What is deep in you is not the sum of your waters,

but the thickness of their pulp, the density of their body.

What lives in you can be encompassed by diving a few meters,

but the eternal—within the brief—needs millennia.


It is what you produce, what gathers at your side.

A distance can be measured, depth can be gauged.

Never the magical dream, the delirium that sweeps away

fugitive realities you reject as inhospitable.


Before you, the fragile avenues

of things disintegrate, and of creatures that are things more than beings.

Your excessive salt sets the ground against the frail plant

to keep it firm, so it may float without care.


You are small and sturdy like an ancient peasant

who came from the lands of Ulysses and Nausicaa.

No one exhausts you, and multitudes of farmers came

to give themselves to you, whom you feed with fish from your ‘corrals.’


Profusely inhabited by precious fauna,

you throb beside fields of almond and olive trees.

Always the same, always together. Indifferent to time.

You are perfect eternity. I came and will go. You will remain.


By remaining, you are deep, as only a sea can be;

as only a sky growing from your mouth can be!

Distance barely counts beside you, sea of mine.

Everything is close and all the same: a great dream with shores.
editorial_note: Translated from the stored Spanish original. The collection-and-date footer is omitted as bibliographic matter. The poem addresses the Mar Menor; its paradoxes of measurable shallowness and eternal depth are preserved.
